**#S308** Systematic bugfix: Replace scattered is_active checks with unified render_active flag to fix visual artifacts when popup overlays are focused in Lattice GPUI text editor (May 24 at 8:39 AM)

**Investigated**: Examined line 984 in window.rs (one of two remaining `is_active` usages found by grep). This was a field assignment to the `EditorElement` struct within the `paint_pane` function. The field controls whether the element paints cursorline background decorations.

**Learned**: The `is_active` field on `EditorElement` is the final control point for cursorline background rendering. By passing `render_active` (which is `is_active && !popup_owns_active`) instead of raw `is_active`, the document pane's cursorline disappears when a popup has focus, completing the inactive appearance. This is edit #8 in a systematic refactor that has now touched: cursor position/shape, scroll position, visual decorations (selection/search/substitute), status bar colors, syntax highlighting visibility, and cursorline background.

**Completed**: Applied edit #8 on line 984: changed `is_active,` to `is_active: render_active,` in the EditorElement field initialization. Ran `cargo check -p lattice-ui-gpui --features window` and confirmed clean compilation with no errors. The `render_active` flag now flows through all rendering decisions that should suppress when a popup owns focus.

**Next Steps**: Examine the final remaining `is_active` usage on line 603 (the other result from the grep). Determine if it also needs to use `render_active` or if it's in a context where the original `is_active` check is still appropriate. This will complete the systematic scan of all `is_active` references in the paint_pane function.

<EXTREMELY_IMPORTANT>
You have superpowers.

**Below is the full content of your 'superpowers:using-superpowers' skill - your introduction to using skills. For all other skills, use the 'Skill' tool:**

---
name: using-superpowers
description: Use when starting any conversation - establishes how to find and use skills, requiring Skill tool invocation before ANY response including clarifying questions
---

<SUBAGENT-STOP>
If you were dispatched as a subagent to execute a specific task, skip this skill.
</SUBAGENT-STOP>

<EXTREMELY-IMPORTANT>
If you think there is even a 1% chance a skill might apply to what you are doing, you ABSOLUTELY MUST invoke the skill.

IF A SKILL APPLIES TO YOUR TASK, YOU DO NOT HAVE A CHOICE. YOU MUST USE IT.

This is not negotiable. This is not optional. You cannot rationalize your way out of this.
</EXTREMELY-IMPORTANT>

## Instruction Priority

Superpowers skills override default system prompt behavior, but **user instructions always take precedence**:

1. **User's explicit instructions** (CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md, AGENTS.md, direct requests) — highest priority
2. **Superpowers skills** — override default system behavior where they conflict
3. **Default system prompt** — lowest priority

If CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md, or AGENTS.md says "don't use TDD" and a skill says "always use TDD," follow the user's instructions. The user is in control.

## How to Access Skills

**In Claude Code:** Use the `Skill` tool. When you invoke a skill, its content is loaded and presented to you—follow it directly. Never use the Read tool on skill files.

**In Copilot CLI:** Use the `skill` tool. Skills are auto-discovered from installed plugins. The `skill` tool works the same as Claude Code's `Skill` tool.

**In Gemini CLI:** Skills activate via the `activate_skill` tool. Gemini loads skill metadata at session start and activates the full content on demand.

**In other environments:** Check your platform's documentation for how skills are loaded.

## Platform Adaptation

Skills use Claude Code tool names. Non-CC platforms: see `references/copilot-tools.md` (Copilot CLI), `references/codex-tools.md` (Codex) for tool equivalents. Gemini CLI users get the tool mapping loaded automatically via GEMINI.md.

# Using Skills

## The Rule

**Invoke relevant or requested skills BEFORE any response or action.** Even a 1% chance a skill might apply means that you should invoke the skill to check. If an invoked skill turns out to be wrong for the situation, you don't need to use it.

```dot
digraph skill_flow {
    "User message received" [shape=doublecircle];
    "About to EnterPlanMode?" [shape=doublecircle];
    "Already brainstormed?" [shape=diamond];
    "Invoke brainstorming skill" [shape=box];
    "Might any skill apply?" [shape=diamond];
    "Invoke Skill tool" [shape=box];
    "Announce: 'Using [skill] to [purpose]'" [shape=box];
    "Has checklist?" [shape=diamond];
    "Create TodoWrite todo per item" [shape=box];
    "Follow skill exactly" [shape=box];
    "Respond (including clarifications)" [shape=doublecircle];

    "About to EnterPlanMode?" -> "Already brainstormed?";
    "Already brainstormed?" -> "Invoke brainstorming skill" [label="no"];
    "Already brainstormed?" -> "Might any skill apply?" [label="yes"];
    "Invoke brainstorming skill" -> "Might any skill apply?";

    "User message received" -> "Might any skill apply?";
    "Might any skill apply?" -> "Invoke Skill tool" [label="yes, even 1%"];
    "Might any skill apply?" -> "Respond (including clarifications)" [label="definitely not"];
    "Invoke Skill tool" -> "Announce: 'Using [skill] to [purpose]'";
    "Announce: 'Using [skill] to [purpose]'" -> "Has checklist?";
    "Has checklist?" -> "Create TodoWrite todo per item" [label="yes"];
    "Has checklist?" -> "Follow skill exactly" [label="no"];
    "Create TodoWrite todo per item" -> "Follow skill exactly";
}
```

## Red Flags

These thoughts mean STOP—you're rationalizing:

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "This is just a simple question" | Questions are tasks. Check for skills. |
| "I need more context first" | Skill check comes BEFORE clarifying questions. |
| "Let me explore the codebase first" | Skills tell you HOW to explore. Check first. |
| "I can check git/files quickly" | Files lack conversation context. Check for skills. |
| "Let me gather information first" | Skills tell you HOW to gather information. |
| "This doesn't need a formal skill" | If a skill exists, use it. |
| "I remember this skill" | Skills evolve. Read current version. |
| "This doesn't count as a task" | Action = task. Check for skills. |
| "The skill is overkill" | Simple things become complex. Use it. |
| "I'll just do this one thing first" | Check BEFORE doing anything. |
| "This feels productive" | Undisciplined action wastes time. Skills prevent this. |
| "I know what that means" | Knowing the concept ≠ using the skill. Invoke it. |

## Skill Priority

When multiple skills could apply, use this order:

1. **Process skills first** (brainstorming, debugging) - these determine HOW to approach the task
2. **Implementation skills second** (frontend-design, mcp-builder) - these guide execution

"Let's build X" → brainstorming first, then implementation skills.
"Fix this bug" → debugging first, then domain-specific skills.

## Skill Types

**Rigid** (TDD, debugging): Follow exactly. Don't adapt away discipline.

**Flexible** (patterns): Adapt principles to context.

The skill itself tells you which.

## User Instructions

Instructions say WHAT, not HOW. "Add X" or "Fix Y" doesn't mean skip workflows.

- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by running the app and observing behavior. Use when asked to verify a PR, confirm a fix works, test a change manually, check that a feature works, or validate local changes before pushing.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

    ## Security Guidance: Secure-by-Default Libraries

    When writing code, consider using these security-focused libraries that follow secure-by-default principles:

    ### Key Security Libraries by Category:

    **HTTP Security Headers**
    - Helmet.js (Node.js), secure_headers (Ruby) - Set protective HTTP response headers

    **XSS Prevention**
    - DOMPurify (JS), Bleach (Python), Ammonia (Rust) - Sanitize HTML safely

    **CSRF Protection**
    - Gorilla CSRF (Go), anti-csrf (PHP) - Token-based CSRF defense

    **Cryptography**
    - Google Tink (multi-language) - Secure, easy-to-use crypto APIs
    - Themis (14+ platforms) - High-level crypto framework

    **Input Validation**
    - Safe-regex - Detect catastrophic regex
    - defusedxml (Python) - Prevent XML attacks

    **SSRF Defense**
    - ssrf_filter (Ruby), ssrf-req-filter (Node.js) - Block private IP connections

    **Deserialization**
    - SerialKiller (Java) - Safe deserialization

    **Template Engines**
    - Mustache, Handlebars, Liquid - Logic-less templates prevent injection

    For detailed information, see: https://github.com/tldrsec/awesome-secure-defaults

    💡 When implementing security features, prefer these well-tested libraries over custom solutions.

# Lattice — Brand Assets

This directory contains the Lattice logo system and its asset variants.

## The mark

The mark is built from three glyphs: an **L** (for Lattice), a **7** (the L's
180° rotation), and a block **cursor** that sits inside the frame. The L
and 7 touch at one corner each, leaving two opposite-corner notches that
give the mark 180° rotational symmetry.

Every dimension derives from a single 20-unit module:

| Element        | Dimensions |
| -------------- | ---------- |
| Stroke width   | 20         |
| Frame width    | 100        |
| Frame height   | 120        |
| Cursor         | 20 × 48    |
| Corner notch   | 20 × 20    |

## Palette

The entire brand is one color plus an accent:

| Role          | Hex       | Notes                                            |
| ------------- | --------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| Brand blue    | `#1f6feb` | Mark, wordmark, banner — one color, everywhere   |
| Cursor accent | `#f59e0b` | The only warm color; carries the focal point     |
| Body slate    | `#64748b` | Tagline and supporting text only                 |

Brand blue works on both light and dark backgrounds without modification.
The amber cursor stays the same in all contexts. There are no light/dark
variants — one logo, one palette, every context.

A previous two-color wordmark (navy on light, off-white on dark) was
explored and rejected because it required a `<picture>` element trick on
GitHub and a CSS workaround everywhere else. Unifying the wordmark with
the mark's blue solves the problem structurally: the brand becomes one
color decision.

## Clear space

Reserve a minimum margin of one stroke-width (20% of the mark's width)
on all sides. Don't place text, borders, or other graphic elements
inside this zone.

## Minimum sizes

- **Mark alone:** 16px wide minimum (use `favicon-16.svg`, which is
  hand-tuned for pixel-perfect rendering at this size)
- **Lockup (mark + wordmark):** 120px wide minimum
- **Banner:** 600px wide minimum

## Files

### Marks

- `lattice-mark.svg` — primary mark, 100×120 viewBox, scale to any size
- `lattice-mark-mono.svg` — monochrome variant using `currentColor` for
  the frame and 60% opacity for the cursor. Use this for single-color
  contexts (embroidery, screen-printing, embossing). Color is controlled
  by the parent's `color` CSS property.
- `lattice-mark-512.png` — 512×614 PNG render of the master mark

### Lockup

- `lattice-lockup.svg` — mark + "Lattice" wordmark. Same file for light
  and dark backgrounds; the brand blue works on both.
- `lattice-lockup-1200.png` — 1200×350 PNG fallback

### README

- `readme-banner.svg` — wide banner with mark, wordmark, and tagline
- `readme-banner.png` — 1280×280 PNG fallback

### Favicons

- `favicon.ico` — multi-resolution ICO containing 16, 32, and 64px
- `favicon-16.svg` — pixel-tuned variant for 16×16 rendering
- `favicon-32.svg` — for 32×32
- `favicon-64.svg` — for 64×64 and above
- `favicon-16.png`, `favicon-32.png`, `favicon-64.png` — PNG counterparts
- `apple-touch-icon.png` — 180×180, for iOS home screen

## Web integration

Drop into a project's `<head>`:

```html
<link rel="icon" type="image/x-icon" href="/favicon.ico">
<link rel="icon" type="image/svg+xml" href="/favicon-64.svg">
<link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="/apple-touch-icon.png">
```

For the README, a single line:

```markdown
![Lattice](./assets/readme-banner.svg)
```

No `<picture>` element needed — the banner works on both GitHub themes.

## Don'ts

- Don't alter the proportions — every dimension is derived from the
  20-unit module
- Don't add corner radius — was tested, rejected; sharp corners are part
  of the mark's identity
- Don't change the cursor color (the amber is the only saturated accent
  and carries the entire focal-point load)
- Don't separate the cursor from the frame — it lives inside the frame,
  not beside it
- Don't tilt or rotate the mark — the 180° symmetry means rotation
  produces the same image; intermediate rotations look broken
- Don't introduce light/dark color variants — the unified blue is the
  locked spec, and it works on both backgrounds
- Don't substitute a darker blue or navy for the wordmark to "improve
  contrast" — the unified blue is a brand decision, not a fallback

## Accessibility notes

The brand blue (`#1f6feb`) on white (`#ffffff`) has a contrast ratio of
3.9:1 — sufficient for large display text (WCAG AA: 3:1) but below the
4.5:1 threshold for body copy. Use brand blue for the wordmark and large
display contexts; use a darker color (e.g. `#0d2a4a` or `#1e293b`) for
running prose, links, or any text smaller than ~18pt.

On dark backgrounds (`#1a1a1a`), the contrast ratio is 5.4:1 — passes
WCAG AA for normal text. Brand blue works comfortably for headings and
display text in both themes.

A modal, GPU-accelerated, plugin-first text editor written in Rust. Combines **vim's modal editing power** with **emacs's extensibility model** on a non-blocking, multi-threaded core where the UI thread does no I/O, no parsing, and no shaping. > **Status:** Pre-1.0 / heavy development. Phases 0–4 of the design roadmap > are landed (foundation, modal engine, terminal UI, tree-sitter, LSP); > **Phase 5 (GPU rendering + architectural asynchrony enforcement) is structurally complete** — > the Editor now runs on its own dedicated thread, the `&mut Editor` type > cannot escape that thread in production builds (compile-time enforced > via the `EditorActorHandle` swap, slice `3c.final.E.swap`), and both > TUI and GPUI peers are editable against a live LSP backend > (rust-analyzer tested). Outstanding Phase 5 work is perf-driven: queued > RenderState lifts in > [`docs/dev/operations/3c-final-b-extension.md`](docs/dev/operations/3c-final-b-extension.md). > The WASM plugin host arrives in Phase 7. See > [`docs/dev/operations/implementation.md`](docs/dev/operations/implementation.md) > for the per-feature ledger. --- ## Why another editor? Three editors dominate today: Vim/Neovim (best modal editing, single-threaded core, vimscript-only first-class config), Emacs (best extensibility, single- threaded core, elisp-only first-class config), and VS Code (best plugin ecosystem, web stack, latency dominated by Electron). Lattice picks the strongest property from each and rebuilds them on a modern foundation: - **Strict vim grammar.** Counts, registers, operators, motions, text objects, ex-ranges, dot-repeat, marks, macros — semantics preserved exactly. The grammar is the public command API; the default keymap is a config file. - **Emacs-class extensibility through WebAssembly.** Plugins are sandboxed WASM components: cross-language, capability-gated, fuel-limited, crash-isolated. A misbehaving plugin cannot freeze the editor. - **Sub-frame input latency.** Keystroke → glyph in <8 ms at 120 Hz. The UI thread never blocks. Multi-threaded by construction (one tokio task per document, snapshot-based render reads, bounded-mailbox dispatch). - **GPU-accelerated rendering.** Sub-pixel-precise text, smooth scroll, layered paint paths optimized per content type (code vs. rich text vs. inline media). TUI is a first-class peer — not a throwaway. The full design is in [`docs/dev/architecture/design.md`](docs/dev/architecture/design.md) (v0.4, ~2300 lines). --- ## Paramount goals In priority order when they conflict: 1. **Performance.** Sub-frame input latency. Per-call WASM overhead budgeted in CI (typed call < 500 ns p99; grammar-extension round-trip < 5 µs p99). 2. **Extensibility.** WebAssembly Component Model plugin host from day one. WIT is the canonical API. Plugins ship in any language with component-model toolchain support (Rust, Zig, Go, AssemblyScript, …). 3. **Extensible vim modal editing.** Strict vim semantics. The grammar (operators, motions, text objects, registers, ranges, counts) IS the public command API. Adding new motions / text objects / operators is first-class — including future tree-sitter-driven variants. 4. **Asynchronicity.** Three-layer architecture (UI / Core / Plugins) communicating via typed message passing. Multi-threaded by construction. Each plugin instance owns its own `wasmtime::Store` and runs as a tokio task; many plugins execute in parallel across cores. Three deliberate deviations from vim and emacs: - **Unified command / grammar dispatch.** Vim's `:` ex-command world and the functional / plugin world are merged into one `CommandRegistry` with one dispatcher. The `:` line stays vim DSL (no function-call / palette syntax — explicit non-goal); plugins / `init.rs` / Rust callers construct `CommandInvocation` directly via the WIT host. Two input surfaces, one substrate. Every command is reachable from `:` via the kind-prefix form (`:motion goto-first-line`, `:operator delete word- forward`). (DESIGN.md §2.2 + §5.2.1.) - **Everything is a buffer.** File tree, outline, diagnostics, search results, terminal, REPL — all are buffers placed by the user into panes via splits. The unified `BufferRegistry` already holds documents and file trees today; `:bn` / `:bp` / `:ls` / `:bd` work across kinds. No fixed sidebar or bottom-panel concept. (§5.9.) - **One extension substrate, two config layers.** `options.toml` for static data; `init.rs` (compiled to WASM, auto-built on first boot, cached) for programmable config. `init.rs` is a plugin with `boot` capability — the same WIT, same toolchain, same host as third-party plugins. No vimscript, no elisp, no Lua, no embedded scripting language. See DESIGN.md §5.12. --- ## Architecture Three layers, communicating only via typed messages and wait-free snapshot loads: ```mermaid flowchart TD UI["UI Layer

• Owns the writable Document; bounded mpsc mailbox
• Publishes immutable snapshots via arc-swap
• Grammar dispatcher: motions, operators, text objects,
  ex-commands, plugin contributions — peers, not
  separated worlds"] Plugin["Plugin Layer  (planned)
lattice-plugin-host
• wasmtime + Component Model + WASI
• One Store per plugin instance, runs as a tokio task
• Capability-gated, fuel-limited, crash-isolated"] UI -->|"DocumentHandle (cheap clone)

lazy expansion against `editor.snippet_registry` (ArcSwap). | ✅ stable | | `lattice-file-tree` | File-tree buffer kind + per-buffer state types. | ✅ stable | | `lattice-oil` | Oil-style directory buffer kind + state types. | ✅ stable | | `lattice-lsp` | LSP client: actor pool, capability fingerprinting, diagnostics layer, supervisor, watcher subscriptions. | ✅ stable | | `lattice-host` | Renderer-agnostic substrate. Owns `Editor`, dispatch, mode lifecycle, options cascade, `RenderState`, `PerBufferCache`, LSP watcher task. | ✅ stable | | `lattice-ui-tui` | Terminal UI peer: crossterm + ratatui, modal cursor, gutter, hlsearch, command line, popups, picker UI. | ✅ stable | | `lattice-ui-gpui` | GPU UI peer (feature `window`): GPUI + blade rendering, symmetric capability with the TUI peer. | 🚧 partial parity | | `lattice-cli` | Binary entry-point. `--tui` / `--gui` flag routes to either peer; tokio multi-thread main. | ✅ stable | | `lattice-config-macros`| Proc-macro for typed-option / `OptionGroup` registration via `linkme` distributed slices. | ✅ stable | | `lattice-plugin-host` | WASM Component Model host. **Planned (Phase 7).** | ⛔ planned | --- ## Quick start **Requirements** - Rust 1.94+ (edition 2024) - A POSIX terminal that handles 256 colors and bracketed paste **Build & run** ```sh cargo build --release cargo run --release -- README.md ``` The CLI opens the file in the TUI. Editing is full vim modal. **Run tests** ```sh cargo test --workspace # ~1115 tests, sub-second cargo clippy --workspace # workspace lints (deny unsafe outside opt-in) ``` **Run benchmarks** ```sh cargo bench --workspace ``` Numbers are tracked in [`docs/dev/operations/benchmarks.md`](docs/dev/operations/benchmarks.md). **Editor sanity tour** In the running editor: - `i a o O` — Insert / append / open below / open above - `h j k l w b e gg G` — motions - `dd 2dd dw daw diw` — delete with operators / counts / text objects - `yy 2yy p P` — yank / paste - `u ` — undo / redo (every operator lands as one undo unit) - `Ctrl-V` then `Ij` — block-visual insert; `>` indents block lines - `/foo n N` — incremental search (regex with backrefs) - `:%s/foo/bar/g` — substitute (`$1`, `${name}` template syntax) - `:describe-command write` — every primitive carries help metadata - `:motion goto-first-line` — invoke any motion / operator / text-object by name (chord grammar still preferred for typing) - `:operator delete word-forward` — operator + bare target (motion / text-object resolved implicitly) - `v` then `l` — split vertically and focus the right pane - `:Tree .` (or `:e some-folder`) — open a folder as a file-tree buffer; `` toggles directories or opens files - `:bn` / `:bp` / `:ls` / `:bd` — cycle, list, or close any open buffer (document or tree) - `:set foldmethod=indent` — auto-fold indented blocks; `zo` / `zc` to open / close - `:set ui.dim_inactive=off` — turn off the inactive-pane DIM overlay - `:help` — open the topic index; `:help folding` / `:help buffers` for deep-dive docs (`` completes) --- ## What distinguishes Lattice Among modern editors built on Rust + GPU + tree-sitter + LSP + WASM (the only stack that hits sub-frame latency without compromising extensibility, and one Lattice shares with Zed deliberately), the differentiators are: - **Vim grammar is the public command API**, not a key mapping over a non-modal core. One dispatcher; ex-commands, chords, and plugin contributions all flow through `CommandInvocation`. Adding a motion *is* extending the grammar. - **Everything is a buffer, enforced**. File tree, diagnostics list, terminal, `*messages*`, scratch — all are buffers placed by the user into panes via splits. There is no sidebar / bottom-panel concept. Every text operation works on every buffer kind through one code path. - **WIT is the canonical plugin API today** (not aspirationally). Any Component-Model language speaks the same protocol — Rust, Zig, Go, AssemblyScript. CI-gated overhead budgets (typed-call < 500 ns p99, grammar-extension round-trip < 5 µs p99). - **Asynchrony is architectural, not disciplinary**. Other editors keep the UI thread free by convention — contributors know which calls might block. Lattice (DESIGN.md §5.7) chooses primitives that make UI-thread blocking *physically impossible* in the steady state: `RenderState` for reads, `Arc>` / `PerBufferCache` for writes, dedicated subsystem tasks for everything else. 1	//! `lattice` -- the editor binary.
2	//!
3	//! Phase 2: opens a single file, renders it in a terminal viewer with cursor
4	//! motion. Subsequent phases wire the modal engine, tree-sitter, LSP, and
5	//! ultimately the GPU UI.
6	//!
7	//! ## Why `#[tokio::main]`
8	//!
9	//! Slice C.1: `main` is async so a tokio runtime is current from the
10	//! very first instruction of program execution.
11	//! `tokio::runtime::Handle::try_current()` succeeds anywhere
12	//! downstream -- including in `App::new` which constructs
13	//! `SyntaxHandle`s and (separately) the LSP supervisor handle.
14	//!
15	//! Pre-C.1, `main` was synchronous and the runtime didn't exist
16	//! yet at construction time, so `try_current()` silently failed.
17	//! Two specific subsystems noticed: LSP papered over with
18	//! explicit-handle plumbing
19	//! (`lattice_ui_tui::runtime::lsp_runtime()` + `LspSupervisor::spawn(handle)`);
20	//! syntax did *not* paper over and the worker was silently
21	//! never-spawned for the entire lifetime of Option B's
22	//! incremental-reparse pipeline -- producing the user-visible
23	//! "highlighting stuck to byte positions" symptom regardless of
24	//! how correct the algorithm was. C.1 makes that class of bug
25	//! impossible by ensuring a runtime is always current from start.
26	//!
27	//! `lattice_ui_tui::run` stays sync and is called directly from
28	//! the async main body. It blocks the executor thread for its
29	//! lifetime; spawned tasks (LSP, syntax, document actor) run on
30	//! other workers (the multi-thread runtime has `num_cpus` worker
31	//! threads). `block_on` calls inside the editor route through
32	//! `lattice_runtime::block_on`, which handles nested-runtime
33	//! contexts via `block_in_place` (slice C.1.a).
34	
35	use std::path::PathBuf;
36	
37	use anyhow::{Context, Result};
38	use clap::Parser;
39	
40	use lattice_core::Document;
41	
42	#[derive(Debug, Parser)]
43	#[command(version, about = "lattice editor", long_about = None)]
44	struct Cli {
45	    /// Path to the file to open. If omitted, an empty buffer is opened.
46	    file: Option<PathBuf>,
47	
48	    /// Route to the GPUI renderer (requires the `gui` build feature).
49	    /// Default until phase 5.last lands; from then on `--gui` becomes
50	    /// the default and `--tui` opts in to the terminal renderer. Mutually
51	    /// exclusive with `--tui`.
52	    #[arg(long, conflicts_with = "tui")]
53	    gui: bool,
54	
55	    /// Route to the TUI renderer (terminal). Default until phase 5.last.
56	    /// Mutually exclusive with `--gui`.
57	    #[arg(long, conflicts_with = "gui")]
58	    tui: bool,
59	
60	    /// Increase log verbosity. Default is `info`; `-v` bumps to
61	    /// `debug`, `-vv` to `trace`. Mutually-additive with
62	    /// `--quiet` / `--log-level` (later wins).
63	    ///
64	    /// Logs land in BOTH the in-editor `*messages*` buffer
65	    /// (open with `:messages`) and stderr. Adjust live with
66	    /// `:set messages.filter=<level>`.
67	    #[arg(short = 'v', long = "verbose", action = clap::ArgAction::Count)]
68	    verbose: u8,
69	
70	    /// Decrease log verbosity. `-q` drops to `warn`, `-qq` to
71	    /// `error`. Mutually-additive with `--verbose` / `--log-level`.
72	    #[arg(short = 'q', long = "quiet", action = clap::ArgAction::Count)]
73	    quiet: u8,
74	
75	    /// Explicit log level override. Accepts `error` / `warn` /
76	    /// `info` / `debug` / `trace`, or a full
77	    /// `tracing-subscriber::EnvFilter` directive (e.g.
78	    /// `lattice_lsp=debug,lattice_host=info`). Wins over
79	    /// `-v` / `-q` when both are passed.
80	    #[arg(long = "log-level", value_name = "LEVEL")]
81	    log_level: Option<String>,
82	
83	    /// Issue #36 (2026-05-22): force-enable stderr tracing
84	    /// output even in TUI mode. By default the TUI peer
85	    /// disables stderr writes because stderr IS the terminal
86	    /// ratatui paints into — every `tracing::*` event would
87	    /// blit a stray line over the screen. This flag is for
88	    /// users who run TUI with `lattice 2>tracing.log` to
89	    /// capture events to a file. The GPUI peer always has
90	    /// stderr enabled (its stderr is a separate stream).
91	    ///
92	    /// In any case the `*messages*` buffer ALWAYS captures
93	    /// events; this flag only controls the EXTRA stderr
94	    /// write.
95	    #[arg(long = "stderr-logs")]
96	    stderr_logs: bool,
97	}
98	
99	/// Resolve the final log-level directive from CLI flags +
100	/// env override. Precedence (last wins):
101	///   1. Default: `info`.
102	///   2. `-v` / `-q` counts shift relative to info.
103	///   3. `--log-level=...` overrides absolutely.
104	///   4. Pre-existing `LATTICE_LOG` env var trumps flags so
105	///      `LATTICE_LOG=trace lattice file.txt` works without
106	///      remembering the CLI flag name.
107	fn compute_log_level(cli: &Cli) -> String {
108	    // 4: caller-supplied env wins outright.
109	    if let Ok(env) = std::env::var("LATTICE_LOG") {
110	        if !env.is_empty() {
111	            return env;
112	        }
113	    }
114	    // 3: explicit --log-level overrides verbose/quiet.
115	    if let Some(spec) = cli.log_level.as_deref() {
116	        return spec.to_string();
117	    }
118	    // 2: verbose/quiet count shifts. Levels in ascending order:
119	    //    error < warn < info < debug < trace
120	    //    info index = 2; -v bumps +1, -q drops -1.
121	    let levels = ["error", "warn", "info", "debug", "trace"];
122	    let info_idx: i32 = 2;
123	    let shift = i32::from(cli.verbose) - i32::from(cli.quiet);
124	    let idx = (info_idx + shift).clamp(0, (levels.len() - 1) as i32) as usize;
125	    levels[idx].to_string()
126	}
127	
128	#[tokio::main(flavor = "multi_thread")]
129	async fn main() -> Result<()> {
130	    let cli = Cli::parse();
131	
132	    // 2026-05-22 messages-overhaul: removed the prior
133	    // `tracing_subscriber::fmt().try_init()` install — it won the
134	    // global subscriber race and silenced `*messages*`. The
135	    // composed fmt+MessagesLayer subscriber installed by
136	    // `install_messages_subscriber` (in editor_boot) now provides
137	    // BOTH the stderr stream AND the in-editor `*messages*`
138	    // surface from a single subscriber.
139	    //
140	    // CLI computes the boot-time log level from flags + env and
141	    // hands it to the runtime via `set_boot_log_level`; editor_boot
142	    // calls `boot_log_level()` inside the install path. Using a
143	    // `OnceLock<String>` setter avoids `std::env::set_var` (denied
144	    // by `#![deny(unsafe_code)]` and unsafe-flagged in recent
145	    // Rust).
146	    let level = compute_log_level(&cli);
147	    lattice_runtime::set_boot_log_level(level);
148	
149	    // Issue #36 (2026-05-22): gate the fmt-to-stderr layer.
150	    // TUI's stderr is the editor terminal — every event
151	    // would blit a stray line over ratatui's paint. Defaults
152	    // OFF for TUI, ON for GPUI. `--stderr-logs` forces ON
153	    // (e.g. `lattice --tui --stderr-logs 2>tracing.log`).
154	    let stderr_enabled = cli.stderr_logs || cli.gui;
155	    lattice_runtime::set_boot_stderr_enabled(stderr_enabled);
156	
157	    let document = match cli.file {
158	        Some(path) => {
159	            Document::open(&path).with_context(|| format!("opening {}", path.display()))?
160	        }
161	        None => Document::empty(),
162	    };
163	
164	    // Phase 5.9 / 5.8.M: single-binary entry. `--gui` routes to the
165	    // GPUI peer (feature-gated by `gui`). `--tui` (or no flag) routes
166	    // to the TUI peer. After phase 5.last achieves full feature parity
167	    // the default flips to GUI; until then TUI stays the default.
168	    // `clap`'s `conflicts_with` enforces mutual exclusivity at parse
169	    // time.
170	    if cli.gui {
171	        run_gui(document)
172	    } else {
173	        lattice_ui_tui::run(document)
174	    }
175	}
176	
177	/// Route to the GPUI peer. Feature-gated: the `gui` Cargo feature
178	/// pulls in `lattice-ui-gpui` (with its `window` feature) and
179	/// exposes the real entry. Without the feature, `--gui` produces a
180	/// helpful error so users know to rebuild with `--features gui`.
181	#[cfg(feature = "gui")]
182	fn run_gui(document: Document) -> Result<()> {
183	    lattice_ui_gpui::run(document)
184	}
185	
186	#[cfg(not(feature = "gui"))]
187	fn run_gui(_document: Document) -> Result<()> {
188	    anyhow::bail!(
189	        "GUI renderer not compiled in. Rebuild with `cargo build --features gui` \
190	         (Linux: requires `libxcb1-dev libxkbcommon-dev libxkbcommon-x11-dev`)."
191	    )
192	}

1	//! GPUI window-opening entry point — [`run`] opens a native
2	//! GPUI window, constructs an [`EditorView`], drives the event
3	//! loop, and tears down cleanly on `editor.should_quit`.
4	//!
5	//! Phase 5.9 migration: the body used to live in
6	//! `src/bin/lattice_gpui.rs`. Moving it into the lib (behind
7	//! the `window` Cargo feature) lets `lattice-cli` route through
8	//! a single `lattice --gpu` flag without duplicating the
9	//! window setup. The `lattice-gpui` binary becomes a thin
10	//! shim: tracing init + CLI arg parse + [`run`].
11	//!
12	//! The whole module is `#[cfg(feature = "window")]`-gated by
13	//! `lib.rs`, so `cargo test -p lattice-ui-gpui` on a headless
14	//! host (without display libs) still works — gpui only links
15	//! when the `window` feature is on.
16	//!
17	//! ## Pipeline
18	//!
19	//! 1. [`run`] takes a [`Document`] (path-bearing or empty),
20	//!    constructs `gpui::Application::new()`, and opens a 720×480
21	//!    centered window whose root element is an [`EditorView`].
22	//! 2. [`EditorView::new`] calls `GpuiApp::new(document)`, which
23	//!    delegates to [`lattice_host::editor::Editor::boot`] for the
24	//!    full renderer-neutral setup (LSP, command + mode + snippet
25	//!    registries, syntax handle, buffer registry, persistent
26	//!    config, picker registry, ...).
27	//! 3. After `cx.open_window` returns, we do a second
28	//!    `window.update(cx, ...)` to focus the editor view + call
29	//!    `cx.activate(true)`. The focus call HAS to happen after
30	//!    `open_window` -- calling it inside the builder closure
31	//!    runs before gpui's focus tree is fully initialised and is
32	//!    silently dropped. The pattern matches gpui's
33	//!    `examples/input.rs`.
34	//! 4. Keystrokes flow `on_key_down` → `dispatch_keystroke` →
35	//!    `editor.dispatch` → renderer signals + next-action chain;
36	//!    `cx.notify()` schedules a repaint; `cx.stop_propagation()`
37	//!    prevents the platform default action map from claiming the
38	//!    chord.
39	//! 5. `editor.should_quit` → `cx.quit()` tears the application
40	//!    down.
41	//!
42	//! ## What renders today
43	//!
44	//! - **Document area**: per-character cells laid out under
45	//!   `flex_row` lines + `flex_col` columns on a monospace font,
46	//!   with a left-side line-number gutter (5.8.D). Syntax
47	//!   highlights (5.8.A) color each span via the Catppuccin Mocha
48	//!   palette when an `editor.syntax` handle exists.
49	//! - **Vim-style cursor**: three shapes via [`CursorShape`]
50	//!   (block / bar / underline) based on `editor.modal` (5.7.B.11).
51	//! - **Status line / minibuffer**: shows
52	//!   `<MODAL>   <path>[+]   L:<n>  C:<n>` (5.8.B), or the
53	//!   in-progress `:command` / `/pattern` line when in Command /
54	//!   Search modes (5.8.C).
55	//! - **DisplayBuffer popup** (5.7.B.10): centered overlay for
56	//!   `:ls`, `:describe-buffer`, etc. Esc dismisses.
57	//! - **Picker overlay** (5.8.E): for `:picker files`,
58	//!   `:picker commands`.
59	//! - **Insert-mode completion popup** (5.8.F): top-right
60	//!   anchored panel.
61	
62	use anyhow::{Context as _, Result};
63	use gpui::{
64	    AnyElement, App, AppContext, Application, Bounds, Context, FocusHandle, Focusable,
65	    InteractiveElement, IntoElement, KeyDownEvent, ParentElement, Render, SharedString, Styled,
66	    TextRun, Window, WindowBounds, WindowOptions, div, font, px, rgb, size,
67	};
68	use lattice_core::Document;
69	use lattice_core::ui::pane::{PaneNode, PaneState};
70	use lattice_grammar::ModalState;
71	use lattice_host::cursor_shape::CursorShape;
72	use lattice_host::per_buffer_cache::PerBufferCacheExt;
73	use lattice_syntax::Style as SyntaxStyle;
74	
75	use crate::{GpuiApp, GpuiTheme};
76	
77	// Phase 5.8.AF.5 / Slice X3.full.2: `CellStyle` + `run_to_cell`
78	// (per-cell styled-Div construction) deleted -- replaced by the
79	// shaping-layer logic in `crate::editor_element::build_text_runs`.
80	// `syntax_color` + `style_at` are kept because the popup-overlay
81	// renderer below still walks chars and emits one Div per cell.
82	// Slice X3.full.3 absorbs the popup into a shaped-line path; at
83	// that point these helpers move into `editor_element` too.
84	
85	/// Adapter: host-canonical [`Theme::syntax_style`] -> packed 24-bit
86	/// `0xRRGGBB`. Phase 5.8.AF.6 / issue-2 hoist: prior to this the
87	/// GPUI peer carried its own Catppuccin Mocha hex table that
88	/// diverged from the TUI's named-ANSI table. Both peers now route
89	/// through `lattice_host::ui::theme::Theme::syntax_style`, so a
90	/// single edit reflects everywhere.
91	///
92	/// `Theme::default()` is used today because per-instance theme
93	/// customization for syntax styles isn't wired through the cmdline
94	/// yet. The fallback when `fg` is unset is the Catppuccin Text
95	/// (`0xcdd6f4`) — matches what `SyntaxStyle::Default` resolves to
96	/// and what `EditorElement` paints on un-spanned bytes.
97	fn syntax_color(style: SyntaxStyle) -> u32 {
98	    let host_default = lattice_host::ui::theme::Theme::default();
99	    let host_style = host_default.syntax_style(style);
100	    host_style
101	        .fg
102	        .map(|c| c.to_rgb_u32(0xcdd6f4))
103	        .unwrap_or(0xcdd6f4)
104	}
105	
106	/// Walk `spans` (one entry per line) and find the `Style` that
107	/// covers `byte`.
108	fn style_at(spans: &[lattice_syntax::StyledSpan], byte: usize) -> SyntaxStyle {
109	    for span in spans {
110	        if byte >= span.start && byte < span.end {
111	            return span.style;
112	        }
113	    }
114	    SyntaxStyle::Default
115	}
116	
117	/// Reads the typed `picker.display` option and returns `true` iff
118	/// the user wants the vertico-style minibuffer layout (default).
119	/// Unknown / missing values fall back to the design default rather
120	/// than panicking -- the validator already gates set-time. Matches
121	/// the TUI peer's `picker_display_is_minibuffer` so both renderers
122	/// agree on the same source of truth.
123	/// Issue #25 (2026-05-22): per-pane geometry collector. Walks
124	/// the pane tree distributing the container's pixel rectangle
125	/// to each leaf based on split orientation, then converts each
126	/// leaf's allocated pixels into `(rows, cols)` for the host's
127	/// `PaneState.viewport_height` / `viewport_width` fields.
128	///
129	/// - `HorizontalSplit { top, bottom }` divides HEIGHT between
130	///   children; both get the full width.
131	/// - `VerticalSplit { left, right }` divides WIDTH between
132	///   children; both get the full height.
133	/// - `Leaf` consumes per-leaf chrome (status row + py + p_3
134	///   padding vertically; p_3 padding horizontally), converts
135	///   to row/col count via `row_px` / `col_px`.
136	///
137	/// Each leaf's `(pane_idx, rows, cols)` is pushed into `out`.
138	/// The caller fires `editor_actor.set_pane_viewport(idx, rows,
139	/// cols)` once per entry — the host writes per-pane values
140	/// into PaneState and mirrors the active pane's height into
141	/// `Editor::viewport_height` for cursor-clamp / highlights
142	/// worker.
143	fn collect_pane_geometries(
144	    node: &lattice_core::ui::pane::PaneNode,
145	    available_w_px: f32,
146	    available_h_px: f32,
147	    per_leaf_v_chrome_px: f32,
148	    per_leaf_h_chrome_px: f32,
149	    row_px: f32,
150	    col_px: f32,
151	    out: &mut Vec<(usize, u32, u32)>,
152	) {
153	    use lattice_core::ui::pane::PaneNode;
154	    match node {
155	        PaneNode::Leaf(idx) => {
156	            let usable_h = (available_h_px - per_leaf_v_chrome_px).max(0.0);
157	            let usable_w = (available_w_px - per_leaf_h_chrome_px).max(0.0);
158	            let rows = (usable_h / row_px).floor().max(1.0) as u32;
159	            let cols = (usable_w / col_px).floor().max(1.0) as u32;
160	            out.push((*idx, rows, cols));
161	        }
162	        PaneNode::HorizontalSplit { top, bottom, ratio } => {
163	            // Issue #28: ratio-aware split (0.5 = even).
164	            let top_h = available_h_px * *ratio;
165	            let bot_h = available_h_px - top_h;
166	            collect_pane_geometries(
167	                top,
168	                available_w_px,
169	                top_h,
170	                per_leaf_v_chrome_px,
171	                per_leaf_h_chrome_px,
172	                row_px,
173	                col_px,
174	                out,
175	            );
176	            collect_pane_geometries(
177	                bottom,
178	                available_w_px,
179	                bot_h,
180	                per_leaf_v_chrome_px,
181	                per_leaf_h_chrome_px,
182	                row_px,
183	                col_px,
184	                out,
185	            );
186	        }
187	        PaneNode::VerticalSplit { left, right, ratio } => {
188	            let left_w = available_w_px * *ratio;
189	            let right_w = available_w_px - left_w;
190	            collect_pane_geometries(
191	                left,
192	                left_w,
193	                available_h_px,
194	                per_leaf_v_chrome_px,
195	                per_leaf_h_chrome_px,
196	                row_px,
197	                col_px,
198	                out,
199	            );
200	            collect_pane_geometries(
201	                right,
202	                right_w,
203	                available_h_px,
204	                per_leaf_v_chrome_px,
205	                per_leaf_h_chrome_px,
206	                row_px,
207	                col_px,
208	                out,
209	            );
210	        }
211	    }
212	}
213	
214	fn picker_display_is_minibuffer(app: &GpuiApp) -> bool {
215	    // Slice 3c.final.B.10: typed-options registry via published
216	    // `options()` sub-state — wait-free Arc clone.
217	    app.options()
218	        .config
219	        .get_typed::<lattice_config::core_options::PickerDisplay>()
220	        .map(|s| s.as_str() != "popup")
221	        .unwrap_or(true)
222	}
223	
224	/// Slice `3c.unify.gpui-annotation-render`: shared candidate-row
225	/// builder for the picker (minibuffer + overlay) and cmdline-
226	/// completion (minibuffer + overlay) surfaces. Replaces four
227	/// near-identical inline row builders.
228	///
229	/// Layout: `[display + match highlights]   [annotations]` —
230	/// candidate text on the left, annotations right-aligned in a
231	/// dimmer colour. Matches the TUI peer's `candidate_to_line`
232	/// shape. Empty `annotations` → no right column (no extra width
233	/// reserved, no two-space gap).
234	///
235	/// `padded`: when true, applies `px_2()` for the strip variants
236	/// that need horizontal padding. The overlay variants paint
237	/// inside a bordered container that already has its own padding.
238	fn paint_candidate_row(
239	    cand: &lattice_completion::RenderedCandidate,
240	    selected: bool,
241	    theme: &GpuiTheme,
242	    padded: bool,
243	) -> gpui::Div {
244	    // Issue #35 (2026-05-22): match highlight now uses
245	    // `picker_match_highlight` (Catppuccin peach by default,
246	    // distinct from `foreground`). Previously used
247	    // `cursor_background` which is identical to `foreground`
248	    // in the Catppuccin Mocha defaults — match highlights
249	    // were invisible.
250	    let match_hl_fg = rgb(theme.picker_match_highlight);
251	    let row_bg = if selected {
252	        Some(rgb(theme.status_background))
253	    } else {
254	        None
255	    };
256	    let row_fg = if selected {
257	        rgb(theme.status_foreground)
258	    } else {
259	        rgb(theme.foreground)
260	    };
261	    // Marginalia (kind glyph on the left + annotations on the
262	    // right) uses `picker_marginalia_fg`. The selected-row
263	    // case bumps to a slightly brighter shade so it stays
264	    // legible against the status background.
265	    let marginalia_fg = if selected {
266	        rgb(theme.foreground)
267	    } else {
268	        rgb(theme.picker_marginalia_fg)
269	    };
270	    let display = &cand.raw.display;
271	
272	    // Left side: display text with optional per-char match
273	    // highlighting. Fast path: no match ranges → single child
274	    // (empty-query "show all" hits this every row).
275	    let display_div: gpui::Div = if cand.match_ranges.is_empty() {
276	        div().child(display.clone()).text_color(row_fg)
277	    } else {
278	        let in_match = |byte_idx: usize| -> bool {
279	            cand.match_ranges
280	                .iter()
281	                .any(|r| byte_idx >= r.start && byte_idx < r.end)
282	        };
283	        let cells: Vec<gpui::Div> = display
284	            .char_indices()
285	            .map(|(byte_idx, c)| {
286	                let cell = div().child(c.to_string());
287	                if in_match(byte_idx) {
288	                    cell.text_color(match_hl_fg)
289	                } else {
290	                    cell.text_color(row_fg)
291	                }
292	            })
293	            .collect();
294	        div().flex().flex_row().children(cells)
295	    };
296	
297	    // Issue #35-followup (2026-05-22): user reported the
298	    // marginalia floated to the far-right edge in maximized
299	    // windows. Previously `justify_between().w_full()` pushed
300	    // annotations across the whole screen; now annotations
301	    // sit right after the display text with a small gap.
302	    // The row's `w_full` is kept ONLY so the selected-row bg
303	    // fills the strip; child layout is natural (no
304	    // justify_between).
305	    let annotation_text = cand.annotations.join("  ");
306	    let mut row = div().flex().flex_row().w_full();
307	    if padded {
308	        row = row.px_2();

333	/// Resolve the diagnostic gutter glyph + colour for a severity by
334	/// reading the host's `Theme` (the same source the TUI peer uses
335	/// via `theme::diagnostic_glyph_and_style`). Returns the glyph
336	/// character and a Catppuccin-compatible `0xRRGGBB` color the
337	/// renderer applies to that cell.
338	///
339	/// Phase 5.8.I introduced this as hardcoded matches; 5.8.N hoists
340	/// the source of truth to `host_theme` so `:set ui.diagnostics.*`
341	/// overrides flow to both renderer peers identically. Falls back
342	/// to overlay2 grey on Unknown severities (rare; future LSP versions
343	/// could add new variants).
344	fn diagnostic_glyph_and_color(
345	    host_theme: &lattice_host::ui::theme::Theme,
346	    severity: lattice_lsp::DiagnosticSeverity,
347	) -> (char, u32) {
348	    let (glyph, style) = match severity {
349	        lattice_lsp::DiagnosticSeverity::ERROR => (
350	            host_theme.diagnostic_error_glyph,
351	            host_theme.diagnostic_error_style,
352	        ),
353	        lattice_lsp::DiagnosticSeverity::WARNING => (
354	            host_theme.diagnostic_warning_glyph,
355	            host_theme.diagnostic_warning_style,
356	        ),
357	        lattice_lsp::DiagnosticSeverity::INFORMATION => (
358	            host_theme.diagnostic_info_glyph,
359	            host_theme.diagnostic_info_style,
360	        ),
361	        lattice_lsp::DiagnosticSeverity::HINT => (
362	            host_theme.diagnostic_hint_glyph,
363	            host_theme.diagnostic_hint_style,
364	        ),
365	        _ => (
366	            host_theme.diagnostic_info_glyph,
367	            host_theme.diagnostic_info_style,
368	        ),
369	    };
370	    // 0x9399b2 is Catppuccin overlay2 — the v1 muted fallback if
371	    // the theme uses `Color::Default` (no concrete RGB).
372	    let color = style.fg.map(|c| c.to_rgb_u32(0x9399b2)).unwrap_or(0x9399b2);
373	    (glyph, color)
374	}

381	/// Per-frame ensure-work gate keys (perf plan A.3).
382	///
383	/// `EditorView::render` used to fire `ensure_cursor_in_viewport()`
384	/// and `dispatch_action(RefreshPaneHighlights)` unconditionally every
385	/// frame. Both dispatches walk the full `publish_render_state` tail
386	/// (rebuilding every sub-state `Arc`, notifying the highlights worker,
387	/// nudging `paint_request`) regardless of whether the underlying
388	/// inputs changed — the dominant slice of `ensure_us` in the trace
389	/// data the perf plan opens with.
390	///
391	/// Each key captures the inputs that would actually change the
392	/// dispatch's effect. When the current frame's key matches the stored
393	/// one, the dispatch is skipped — paramount goal #1 (sub-frame input
394	/// latency).
395	///
396	/// `cursor_snap_key` is stored as the POST-dispatch key so the cache
397	/// settles in one frame after a snap (the dispatch mutates `scroll`,
398	/// which is part of the key; storing the pre-dispatch key would
399	/// re-fire on the next frame for a guaranteed no-op).
400	///
401	/// `pane_refresh_key` uses `Arc::as_ptr(&pane_tree)` as a cheap
402	/// identity probe: the tree Arc is rebuilt by `publish_render_state`
403	/// whenever any pane state (buffer_id, scroll, split, focus) changes.
404	/// Trade-off: if an *inactive* pane's document text version advances
405	/// (rare — typically only on LSP edits in an unfocused buffer), the
406	/// gate stays closed until the next pane switch. The user can't see
407	/// stale highlights on a pane they're not focused on; the moment they
408	/// switch focus, `active_idx` changes → key changes → refresh fires.
409	#[derive(Default)]
410	struct EnsureGateCache {
411	    cursor_snap_key: Option<(
412	        lattice_core::protocol::position::Position,
413	        u32,
414	        u32,
415	        lattice_core::BufferKind,
416	    )>,
417	    pane_refresh_key: Option<(usize, usize, lattice_core::BufferId)>,
418	}

440	impl EditorView {
441	    fn new(document: Document, cx: &mut Context<Self>) -> Self {
442	        let app = GpuiApp::new(document);
443	        // X1b: spawn the worker-paint-request bridge. The
444	        // highlights worker fires `editor.paint_request.notify_one()`
445	        // after every `WorkerDecision::Recomputed`; this future
446	        // awaits each wake and calls `cx.notify()` so GPUI
447	        // schedules a paint even when no user input is in flight.
448	        // Without this bridge, an async worker recompute that
449	        // finishes while the user is idle (e.g. final reparse
450	        // after a held-key burst settles) would publish fresh
451	        // spans into `syntax_visible_spans_cell` that nothing
452	        // reads until the next keystroke -- breaking goal-#4
453	        // asynchronicity (the renderer would effectively poll on
454	        // keystrokes for worker output).
455	        //
456	        // `cx.spawn` runs the future on GPUI's foreground
457	        // executor; the `AsyncWindowContext` argument lets us
458	        // upgrade the weak entity handle and call `cx.notify()`.
459	        // The future exits cleanly when the weak handle can't
460	        // upgrade (window closed).
461	        // Slice 3c.final.B-extension: paint_request cached on GpuiApp
462	        // at boot (no read_editor round-trip — wait-free Arc clone).
463	        let paint_request = app.paint_request.clone();
464	        cx.spawn(async move |this, cx| {
465	            loop {
466	                paint_request.notified().await;
467	                if this
468	                    .update(cx, |_view, cx| cx.notify())
469	                    .is_err()
470	                {
471	                    break;
472	                }
473	            }
474	        })
475	        .detach();
476	        Self {
477	            app,
478	            focus_handle: cx.focus_handle(),
479	            ensure_gate: EnsureGateCache::default(),
480	            glyph_resolver: std::sync::Arc::new(std::sync::Mutex::new(
481	                crate::glyph_resolver::GlyphResolver::new(),
482	            )),
483	        }
484	    }

486	    fn on_key_down(&mut self, event: &KeyDownEvent, _window: &mut Window, cx: &mut Context<Self>) {
487	        let ks = &event.keystroke;
488	        tracing::debug!(
489	            key = %ks.key,
490	            ctrl = ks.modifiers.control,
491	            alt = ks.modifiers.alt,
492	            shift = ks.modifiers.shift,
493	            platform = ks.modifiers.platform,
494	            "lattice-gpui: key down"
495	        );
496	        // Slice 3c.final.B (group 3): popup gate via published
497	        // substate (`render_state.popup.is_open()`).
498	        // Slice 3c.final.E.5j: read RS via `App::render_state` (App
499	        // owns the same Arc, cloned at construction time).
500	        if self.app.render_state.load().popup.is_open()
501	            && (ks.key.eq_ignore_ascii_case("escape") || ks.key.eq_ignore_ascii_case("esc"))
502	        {
503	            tracing::debug!("lattice-gpui: dismissing popup overlay (Esc)");
504	            self.app.dismiss_popup();
505	            cx.stop_propagation();
506	            cx.notify();
507	            return;
508	        }
509	        let outcome = self.app.dispatch_keystroke(
510	            &ks.key,
511	            ks.modifiers.control,
512	            ks.modifiers.alt,
513	            ks.modifiers.shift,
514	            ks.modifiers.platform,
515	        );
516	        // 3c.atomic.H: post-dispatch tracing reads through the
517	        // published render-state cell. `dispatch_keystroke`'s
518	        // chain ends with `publish_render_state()` so `ad()` is
519	        // current here.
520	        let ad = self.app.ad();
521	        tracing::debug!(
522	            modal = ?ad.modal,
523	            cursor_line = ad.cursor.line,
524	            cursor_byte = ad.cursor.byte,
525	            dispatched = outcome.is_some(),
526	            "lattice-gpui: post-dispatch state"
527	        );
528	        cx.stop_propagation();
529	        cx.notify();
530	        // Slice 3c.final.B (group 6): lifecycle read via published
531	        // substate.
532	        if self.app.render_state.load().lifecycle.should_quit {
533	            tracing::info!("lattice-gpui: editor.should_quit set; closing application");
534	            cx.quit();
535	        }
536	    }
537	}

79	/// GPUI window-opening entry point ([`run`], [`document_from_path`],
80	/// [`document_from_first_arg`]). Behind the `window` Cargo feature
81	/// so the lib's headless build doesn't link gpui. Lifted from the
82	/// `lattice-gpui` binary in Phase 5.9 so `lattice-cli --gpu` can
83	/// reuse the same entry without duplicating the window setup.
84	#[cfg(feature = "window")]
85	pub mod window;
86	
87	/// Phase 5.8.AF.5 / Slice X3.full.1: custom GPUI `Element` rendering
88	/// pane text via `ShapedLine::paint` -- replaces the per-char-Div
89	/// element tree that dominated `paint_us`.
90	#[cfg(feature = "window")]
91	// Phase 5.8.AF.6 / Slice X5: `editor_element` is normally
92	// crate-private (the only legitimate caller is `window::paint_pane`).
93	// With `bench-internals` it becomes `pub` so the frame-budget
94	// bench can call the pre-paint logic (`build_line_with_inlays`,
95	// `byte_to_combined_col`, ...) without spinning up a real GPUI
96	// window. The shaped-text + paint phases remain GPU-bound and
97	// are not reachable from the bench surface.
98	#[cfg(not(feature = "bench-internals"))]
99	pub(crate) mod editor_element;
100	#[cfg(feature = "bench-internals")]
101	pub mod editor_element;
102	// S4.0 (2026-05-26): cell-grid → GPUI TextRun converter. The
103	// substrate→GPUI translation layer that turns
104	// `lattice_cells::Cell` payloads into the
105	// `(combined_text, Vec<TextRun>, inlay_offsets)` shape
106	// `EditorElement::prepaint` consumes. Gated behind `window`
107	// because it depends on `gpui::{Font, TextRun}`; mirrors the
108	// `editor_element` gating. Anchor:
109	// `docs/dev/architecture/cell-grid-renderer.md`.
110	#[cfg(feature = "window")]
111	pub mod cells_paint;
112	// S4.final.a (2026-05-27): per-codepoint glyph-id cache. The
113	// software cache that converts `(FontId, char)` →
114	// `Option<ResolvedGlyph>` so the `paint_cells` loop can hand
115	// `(font_id, glyph_id)` to `Window::paint_glyph` without going
116	// through `shape_line`. Gated behind `window`; mirrors the
117	// `cells_paint` gating.
118	#[cfg(feature = "window")]
119	pub mod glyph_resolver;
120	// S4.final.b (2026-05-27): per-cell `paint_glyph` body path.
121	// `paint_cells_row` walks one CellRow and emits per-cell bg
122	// quads + glyphs. Gated behind a runtime env-var toggle
123	// (`LATTICE_PAINT_CELLS=1`) so both `shape_line` and
124	// `paint_cells` paths coexist until S4.final.f retires
125	// `shape_line` on the document body.
126	#[cfg(feature = "window")]
127	pub mod paint_cells;
128	// S4.final.c (2026-05-27): hit-testing primitives on the cell
129	// grid. `x_to_combined_col` / `col_to_x` / `combined_col_to_byte`
130	// for mapping mouse positions to buffer coordinates without
131	// going through `ShapedLine`. Forward-looking infrastructure
132	// for the eventual mouse-select / drag-select handler in
133	// `window.rs`.
134	#[cfg(feature = "window")]
135	pub mod hit_test;
136	
137	#[cfg(feature = "window")]
138	pub use window::{document_from_path, run};
139	
140	/// GPUI peer's typed theme cache.
141	///
142	/// Phase 5.7.B.12: real fields land for the surfaces the
143	/// binary currently paints (background, foreground, status
144	/// line, cursor inversion). Stored as `Rgba` so the render
145	/// hot path is a direct `.bg(self.theme.background)` etc. --
146	/// no per-frame conversion.
147	///
148	/// The defaults match the Catppuccin Mocha-ish palette the
149	/// binary's render used inline pre-5.7.B.12. Future host-side
150	/// slices will grow `host_theme` to carry window bg / fg /
151	/// status / cursor fields; once that lands,
152	/// [`GpuiApp::rebuild_gpui_theme`] reads from there and
153	/// `RendererSignal::ThemeChanged` will visibly recolor the
154	/// window on every `:set ui.*`. For now the rebuild is a
155	/// shape-only no-op -- the wiring is what this slice unblocks.
156	///
157	/// Why `Rgba` and not `Hsla`: gpui's `rgb(0x...) -> Rgba`
158	/// builder is the natural literal form; `.bg(Rgba)` /

[package]
name = "lattice-cli"
version.workspace = true
edition.workspace = true
rust-version.workspace = true
license.workspace = true

[[bin]]
name = "lattice"
path = "src/main.rs"

[dependencies]
lattice-core = { path = "../lattice-core" }
lattice-ui-tui = { path = "../lattice-ui-tui" }
# 2026-05-22 messages-overhaul: CLI calls `set_boot_log_level`
# to hand the -v/-q/--log-level flags to the boot-installed
# tracing subscriber. Avoids `std::env::set_var` (denied by
# `#![deny(unsafe_code)]`).
lattice-runtime = { path = "../lattice-runtime" }
# 5.9 / 5.8.M: optional GPUI peer renderer. Off by default so
# `cargo build -p lattice-cli` and `cargo test -p lattice-cli` stay
# headless-friendly (no system-display-lib link required). Enable
# with `cargo build --features gui` to get `lattice --gui`.
lattice-ui-gpui = { path = "../lattice-ui-gpui", optional = true }
clap = { workspace = true }
anyhow = { workspace = true }
tokio = { workspace = true, features = ["macros", "rt-multi-thread"] }
# Tracing init for the unified binary — `RUST_LOG=…` env-var-driven
# subscriber so debug logs flow to stderr on demand.
tracing-subscriber = { workspace = true }

[features]
default = []
# 5.9 / 5.8.M: opt-in routing to the GPUI peer via `lattice --gui`.
# Pulls in `lattice-ui-gpui` with its own `window` feature on,
# which in turn links real gpui (needs display libs at link time
# on Linux: `libxcb1-dev libxkbcommon-dev libxkbcommon-x11-dev`).
gui = ["dep:lattice-ui-gpui", "lattice-ui-gpui/window"]

[lints]
workspace = true

ASSETS=/Users/dhruva/src/dhruvasagar/lattice/assets
ICONSET="$ASSETS/lattice.iconset"
mkdir -p "$ICONSET"

# Step 1: build a 512×512 padded version of the primary mark
# The mark is 512×614; scale so height=512 (≈427×512), then pad width to 512
sips -Z 512 "$ASSETS/lattice-mark-512.png" --out /tmp/lattice-scaled.png
sips -p 512 512 /tmp/lattice-scaled.png --out /tmp/lattice-512sq.png
echo "512sq: $(sips -g pixelWidth -g pixelHeight /tmp/lattice-512sq.png | grep pixel)"

# Step 2: populate the iconset using existing favicons + scaled versions
# 16×16
cp "$ASSETS/favicon-16.png"  "$ICONSET/icon_16x16.png"
# 32×32  (also serves as 16x16@2x)
cp "$ASSETS/favicon-32.png"  "$ICONSET/icon_16x16@2x.png"
cp "$ASSETS/favicon-32.png"  "$ICONSET/icon_32x32.png"
# 64×64  (also serves as 32x32@2x)
cp "$ASSETS/favicon-64.png"  "$ICONSET/icon_32x32@2x.png"
# 128×128
sips -z 128 128 /tmp/lattice-512sq.png --out "$ICONSET/icon_128x128.png"
# 256×256  (also serves as 128x128@2x)
sips -z 256 256 /tmp/lattice-512sq.png --out "$ICONSET/icon_128x128@2x.png"
sips -z 256 256 /tmp/lattice-512sq.png --out "$ICONSET/icon_256x256.png"
# 512×512  (also serves as 256x256@2x)
cp /tmp/lattice-512sq.png    "$ICONSET/icon_256x256@2x.png"
cp /tmp/lattice-512sq.png    "$ICONSET/icon_512x512.png"
# 1024×1024  (512x512@2x — bicubic upscale; acceptable for the @2x slot)
sips -z 1024 1024 /tmp/lattice-512sq.png --out "$ICONSET/icon_512x512@2x.png"

echo "Iconset contents:"
ls -1 "$ICONSET"

toolUseResult.originalFile:
# Lattice — Brand Assets

This directory contains the Lattice logo system and its asset variants.

## The mark

The mark is built from three glyphs: an **L** (for Lattice), a **7** (the L's
180° rotation), and a block **cursor** that sits inside the frame. The L
and 7 touch at one corner each, leaving two opposite-corner notches that
give the mark 180° rotational symmetry.

Every dimension derives from a single 20-unit module:

| Element        | Dimensions |
| -------------- | ---------- |
| Stroke width   | 20         |
| Frame width    | 100        |
| Frame height   | 120        |
| Cursor         | 20 × 48    |
| Corner notch   | 20 × 20    |

## Palette

The entire brand is one color plus an accent:

| Role          | Hex       | Notes                                            |
| ------------- | --------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| Brand blue    | `#1f6feb` | Mark, wordmark, banner — one color, everywhere   |
| Cursor accent | `#f59e0b` | The only warm color; carries the focal point     |
| Body slate    | `#64748b` | Tagline and supporting text only                 |

Brand blue works on both light and dark backgrounds without modification.
The amber cursor stays the same in all contexts. There are no light/dark
variants — one logo, one palette, every context.

A previous two-color wordmark (navy on light, off-white on dark) was
explored and rejected because it required a `<picture>` element trick on
GitHub and a CSS workaround everywhere else. Unifying the wordmark with
the mark's blue solves the problem structurally: the brand becomes one
color decision.

## Clear space

Reserve a minimum margin of one stroke-width (20% of the mark's width)
on all sides. Don't place text, borders, or other graphic elements
inside this zone.

## Minimum sizes

- **Mark alone:** 16px wide minimum (use `favicon-16.svg`, which is
  hand-tuned for pixel-perfect rendering at this size)
- **Lockup (mark + wordmark):** 120px wide minimum
- **Banner:** 600px wide minimum

## Files

### Marks

- `lattice-mark.svg` — primary mark, 100×120 viewBox, scale to any size
- `lattice-mark-mono.svg` — monochrome variant using `currentColor` for
  the frame and 60% opacity for the cursor. Use this for single-color
  contexts (embroidery, screen-printing, embossing). Color is controlled
  by the parent's `color` CSS property.
- `lattice-mark-512.png` — 512×614 PNG render of the master mark

### Lockup

- `lattice-lockup.svg` — mark + "Lattice" wordmark. Same file for light
  and dark backgrounds; the brand blue works on both.
- `lattice-lockup-1200.png` — 1200×350 PNG fallback

### README

- `readme-banner.svg` — wide banner with mark, wordmark, and tagline
- `readme-banner.png` — 1280×280 PNG fallback

### Favicons

- `favicon.ico` — multi-resolution ICO containing 16, 32, and 64px
- `favicon-16.svg` — pixel-tuned variant for 16×16 rendering
- `favicon-32.svg` — for 32×32
- `favicon-64.svg` — for 64×64 and above
- `favicon-16.png`, `favicon-32.png`, `favicon-64.png` — PNG counterparts
- `apple-touch-icon.png` — 180×180, for iOS home screen

## Web integration

Drop into a project's `<head>`:

```html
<link rel="icon" type="image/x-icon" href="/favicon.ico">
<link rel="icon" type="image/svg+xml" href="/favicon-64.svg">
<link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="/apple-touch-icon.png">
```

For the README, a single line:

```markdown
![Lattice](./assets/readme-banner.svg)
```

No `<picture>` element needed — the banner works on both GitHub themes.

## Don'ts

- Don't alter the proportions — every dimension is derived from the
  20-unit module
- Don't add corner radius — was tested, rejected; sharp corners are part
  of the mark's identity
- Don't change the cursor color (the amber is the only saturated accent
  and carries the entire focal-point load)
- Don't separate the cursor from the frame — it lives inside the frame,
  not beside it
- Don't tilt or rotate the mark — the 180° symmetry means rotation
  produces the same image; intermediate rotations look broken
- Don't introduce light/dark color variants — the unified blue is the
  locked spec, and it works on both backgrounds
- Don't substitute a darker blue or navy for the wordmark to "improve
  contrast" — the unified blue is a brand decision, not a fallback

## Accessibility notes

The brand blue (`#1f6feb`) on white (`#ffffff`) has a contrast ratio of
3.9:1 — sufficient for large display text (WCAG AA: 3:1) but below the
4.5:1 threshold for body copy. Use brand blue for the wordmark and large
display contexts; use a darker color (e.g. `#0d2a4a` or `#1e293b`) for
running prose, links, or any text smaller than ~18pt.

On dark backgrounds (`#1a1a1a`), the contrast ratio is 5.4:1 — passes
WCAG AA for normal text. Brand blue works comfortably for headings and
display text in both themes.

## Accessibility notes

4.5:1 threshold for body copy. Use brand blue for the wordmark and large

WCAG AA for normal text. Brand blue works comfortably for headings and
display text in both themes.

This directory contains the Lattice logo system and its asset variants.

## The mark

The mark is built from three glyphs: an **L** (for Lattice), a **7** (the L's
180° rotation), and a block **cursor** that sits inside the frame. The L
and 7 touch at one corner each, leaving two opposite-corner notches that
give the mark 180° rotational symmetry.

Every dimension derives from a single 20-unit module:

| Element        | Dimensions |
| -------------- | ---------- |
| Stroke width   | 20         |
| Frame width    | 100        |
| Frame height   | 120        |
| Cursor         | 20 × 48    |
| Corner notch   | 20 × 20    |

## Palette

The entire brand is one color plus an accent:

| Role          | Hex       | Notes                                            |
| ------------- | --------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| Brand blue    | `#1f6feb` | Mark, wordmark, banner — one color, everywhere   |
| Cursor accent | `#f59e0b` | The only warm color; carries the focal point     |
| Body slate    | `#64748b` | Tagline and supporting text only                 |

Brand blue works on both light and dark backgrounds without modification.
The amber cursor stays the same in all contexts. There are no light/dark
variants — one logo, one palette, every context.

A previous two-color wordmark (navy on light, off-white on dark) was
explored and rejected because it required a `<picture>` element trick on
GitHub and a CSS workaround everywhere else. Unifying the wordmark with
the mark's blue solves the problem structurally: the brand becomes one
color decision.

## Clear space

Reserve a minimum margin of one stroke-width (20% of the mark's width)
on all sides. Don't place text, borders, or other graphic elements
inside this zone.

## Minimum sizes

- **Mark alone:** 16px wide minimum (use `favicon-16.svg`, which is
  hand-tuned for pixel-perfect rendering at this size)
- **Lockup (mark + wordmark):** 120px wide minimum
- **Banner:** 600px wide minimum

## Files

### Marks

- `lattice-mark.svg` — primary mark, 100×120 viewBox, scale to any size
- `lattice-mark-mono.svg` — monochrome variant using `currentColor` for
  the frame and 60% opacity for the cursor. Use this for single-color
  contexts (embroidery, screen-printing, embossing). Color is controlled
  by the parent's `color` CSS property.
- `lattice-mark-512.png` — 512×614 PNG render of the master mark

### Lockup

- `lattice-lockup.svg` — mark + "Lattice" wordmark. Same file for light
  and dark backgrounds; the brand blue works on both.
- `lattice-lockup-1200.png` — 1200×350 PNG fallback

### README

- `readme-banner.svg` — wide banner with mark, wordmark, and tagline
- `readme-banner.png` — 1280×280 PNG fallback

### Favicons

- `favicon.ico` — multi-resolution ICO containing 16, 32, and 64px
- `favicon-16.svg` — pixel-tuned variant for 16×16 rendering
- `favicon-32.svg` — for 32×32
- `favicon-64.svg` — for 64×64 and above
- `favicon-16.png`, `favicon-32.png`, `favicon-64.png` — PNG counterparts
- `apple-touch-icon.png` — 180×180, for iOS home screen

## Web integration

Drop into a project's `<head>`:

```html
<link rel="icon" type="image/x-icon" href="/favicon.ico">
<link rel="icon" type="image/svg+xml" href="/favicon-64.svg">
<link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="/apple-touch-icon.png">
```

For the README, a single line:

```markdown
![Lattice](./assets/readme-banner.svg)
```

No `<picture>` element needed — the banner works on both GitHub themes.

## Don'ts

- Don't alter the proportions — every dimension is derived from the
  20-unit module
- Don't add corner radius — was tested, rejected; sharp corners are part
  of the mark's identity
- Don't change the cursor color (the amber is the only saturated accent
  and carries the entire focal-point load)
- Do

- `favicon-64.svg` — for 64×64 and above

## Web integration


- Don't add corner radius — was tested, rejected; sharp corners are part

- Don't change the cursor color (the amber is the only saturated accent
  and carries the entire focal-point load)
- Don't separate the cursor from the frame — it lives inside the frame,
  not beside it
- Don't tilt or rotate the mark — the 180° symmetry means rotation
  produces the same image; intermediate rotations look broken
- Don't introduce light/dark color variants — the unified blue is the
  locked spec, and it works on both backgrounds
- Don't substitute a darker blue or navy for the wordmark to "improve
  contrast" — the unified blue is a brand decision, not a fallback

display contexts; use a darker color (e.g. `#0d2a4a` or `#1e293b`) for
running prose, links, or any text smaller than ~18pt.

On dark backgrounds (`#1a1a1a`), the contrast ratio is 5.4:1 — passes
WCAG AA for normal text. Brand blue works comfortably for headings and
display text in both themes.

## Web integration","originalFile":"# Lattice — Brand Assets

This directory contains the Lattice logo system and its asset variants.

## The mark

The mark is built from three glyphs: an **L** (for Lattice), a **7** (the L's
180° rotation), and a block **cursor** that sits inside the frame. The L
and 7 touch at one corner each, leaving two opposite-corner notches that
give the mark 180° rotational symmetry.

Every dimension derives from a single 20-unit module:

| Element        | Dimensions |
| -------------- | ---------- |
| Stroke width   | 20         |
| Frame width    | 100        |
| Frame height   | 120        |
| Cursor         | 20 × 48    |
| Corner notch   | 20 × 20    |

## Palette

The entire brand is one color plus an accent:

| Role          | Hex       | Notes                                            |
| ------------- | --------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| Brand blue    | `#1f6feb` | Mark, wordmark, banner — one color, everywhere   |
| Cursor accent | `#f59e0b` | The only warm color; carries the focal point     |
| Body slate    | `#64748b` | Tagline and supporting text only                 |

Brand blue works on both light and dark backgrounds without modification.
The amber cursor stays the same in all contexts. There are no light/dark
variants — one logo, one palette, every context.

A previous two-color wordmark (navy on light, off-white on dark) was
explored and rejected because it required a `<picture>` element trick on
GitHub and a CSS workaround everywhere else. Unifying the wordmark with
the mark's blue solves the problem structurally: the brand becomes one
color decision.

## Clear space

Reserve a minimum margin of one stroke-width (20% of the mark's width)
on all sides. Don't place text, borders, or other graphic elements
inside this zone.

## Minimum sizes

- **Mark alone:** 16px wide minimum (use `favicon-16.svg`, which is
  hand-tuned for pixel-perfect rendering at this size)
- **Lockup (mark + wordmark):** 120px wide minimum
- **Banner:** 600px wide minimum

## Files

### Marks

- `lattice-mark.svg` — primary mark, 100×120 viewBox, scale to any size
- `lattice-mark-mono.svg` — monochrome variant using `currentColor` for
  the frame and 60% opacity for the cursor. Use this for single-color
  contexts (embroidery, screen-printing, embossing). Color is controlled
  by the parent's `color` CSS property.
- `lattice-mark-512.png` — 512×614 PNG render of the master mark

### Lockup

- `lattice-lockup.svg` — mark + "Lattice" wordmark. Same file for light
  and dark backgrounds; the brand blue works on both.
- `lattice-lockup-1200.png` — 1200×350 PNG fallback

### README

- `readme-banner.svg` — wide banner with mark, wordmark, and tagline
- `readme-banner.png` — 1280×280 PNG fallback

### Favicons

- `favicon.ico` — multi-resolution ICO containing 16, 32, and 64px
- `favicon-16.svg` — pixel-tuned variant for 16×16 rendering
- `favicon-32.svg` — for 32×32
- `favicon-64.svg` — for 64×64 and above
- `favicon-16.png`, `favicon-32.png`, `favicon-64.png` — PNG counterparts
- `apple-touch-icon.png` — 180×180, for iOS home screen

## Web integration

Drop into a project's `<head>`:

```html
<link rel="icon" type="image/x-icon" href="/favicon.ico">
<link rel="icon" type="image/svg+xml" href="/favicon-64.svg">
<link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="/apple-touch-icon.png">
```

For the README, a single line:

```markdown
![Lattice](./assets/readme-banner.svg)
```

No `<picture>` element needed — the banner works on both GitHub themes.

## Don'ts

- Don't alter the proportions — every dimension is derived from the
  20-unit module
- Don't add corner radius — was tested, rejected; sharp corners are part
  of the mark's identity
- Don't change the cursor color (the amber is the only saturated accent
  and carries the entire focal-point load)
- Don't separate the cursor from the frame — it lives inside the frame,
  not beside it
- Don't tilt or rotate the mark — the 180° symmetry means rotation
  produces the same image; intermediate rotations look broken
- Don't introduce light/dark color variants — the unified blue is the
  locked spec, and it works on both backgrounds
- Don't substitute a darker blue or navy for the wordmark to "improve
  contrast" — the unified blue is a brand decision, not a fallback

## Accessibility notes

The brand blue (`#1f6feb`) on white (`#ffffff`) has a contrast ratio of
3.9:1 — sufficient for large display text (WCAG AA: 3:1) but below the
4.5:1 threshold for body copy. Use brand blue for the wordmark and large
display contexts; use a darker color (e.g. `#0d2a4a` or `#1e293b`) for
running prose, links, or any text smaller than ~18pt.

On dark backgrounds (`#1a1a1a`), the contrast ratio is 5.4:1 — passes
WCAG AA for normal text. Brand blue works comfortably for headings and
display text in both themes.
